title: Routing and the route back
summary: Routing tables, longest-prefix match, default gateways, and why replies need a route too.

steps.title: The routing table
body: Real networks are many networks joined by **routers**:
Every host, not only routers, has a routing table (`ip route`). Each line says "to reach *this network*, send packets *this way*":
10.12.1.0/24 dev eth0 scope link      # my own network: deliver directly
default via 10.12.1.254 dev eth0      # everything else: hand to this router
For each packet the kernel picks the **most specific** matching line (**longest prefix**). `default` is `0.0.0.0/0`: it matches everything, so it's used only when nothing better does.
The router after `via` is the **next hop**, and it must be on a network the host is directly connected to.

steps.prompt: The table has `10.12.1.0/24 dev eth0`, `10.12.0.0/16 via 10.12.1.1` and `default via 10.12.1.254`. Which line carries each destination?
steps.explain: All three match `10.12.1.77`, but /24 is the longest prefix. `10.13.0.1` is outside 10.12.0.0/16, so only default matches.

steps.prompt: Complete the commands: give the client a default gateway, then add a specific route to the DMZ.
steps.explain: `via` names the next hop. `default` is shorthand for 0.0.0.0/0.

steps.title: A route back
body: A ping is two packets, a request and a reply, and **each is routed independently** by whichever host holds it.
If the client can reach the server but the server has no route to the client's network, the request arrives and **the reply is dropped on the server**.
From the client, that looks exactly like the server being dead.
To see how far packets get, capture on the router while pinging:
tcpdump -ni any icmp      # -n: no name lookups, -i any: every interface
traceroute -n 10.12.2.10  # each router on the way
> **Try it for real:** the live lab *Routers and static routes* on the Labs page (needs Docker).

steps.prompt: You ping `10.12.2.10` from the client. On the router, `tcpdump -ni any icmp` shows `ICMP echo request` leaving towards the server, and nothing else. Most likely cause?
options: The server has no route back to 10.12.1.0/24 (no default gateway)
The client has no default gateway
steps.explain: The request got through the router, so the client and router are fine. The reply never comes back, so look at the server's routing table.

steps.prompt: Order a sensible troubleshooting pass for *server doesn't answer ping*.
lines: Check the client's `ip route` for a path to the server
Capture on the router with `tcpdump -ni any icmp`
Check the server's `ip route` for a path back
Fix the missing route and ping again
steps.explain: Work outward hop by hop, and always check the return path.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The router you hand the packet to

steps.title: Longest prefix match
prompt: Write `string Lookup(List<(string Cidr, string Via)> routes, string dst)` returning the `Via` of the most specific route containing `dst`,
or `"unreachable"` if none matches. `Via` is a next-hop IP or `"direct"`. Include `ToUInt`; `/0` must work.
starter: string Lookup(List<(string Cidr, string Via)> routes, string dst)
solution: if (!int.TryParse(p, out int n) || n < 0 || n > 255) throw new FormatException("bad octet " + p);
string Lookup(List<(string Cidr, string Via)> routes, string dst)
template: Dojo.Eq("no default", "unreachable", Lookup(new List<(string Cidr, string Via)> { ("10.12.1.0/24", "direct") }, "10.12.2.10"));
hints: For each route, check containment with a mask and keep the one with the biggest prefix.

steps.title: Both directions
prompt: Write `string Ping(List<(string Cidr, string Via)> clientRoutes, List<(string Cidr, string Via)> serverRoutes, string clientIp, string serverIp)`
using your `Lookup`. Assume the router in between forwards everything. Return:
- `"no route there"` if the client's lookup for `serverIp` is unreachable,
- `"no route back"` if the server's lookup for `clientIp` is unreachable,
starter: string Ping(List<(string Cidr, string Via)> clientRoutes, List<(string Cidr, string Via)> serverRoutes, string clientIp, string serverIp)
solution: if (!int.TryParse(p, out int n) || n < 0 || n > 255) throw new FormatException("bad octet " + p);
string Lookup(List<(string Cidr, string Via)> routes, string dst)
string Ping(List<(string Cidr, string Via)> clientRoutes, List<(string Cidr, string Via)> serverRoutes, string clientIp, string serverIp)
template: var dojoC = new List<(string Cidr, string Via)> { ("10.12.1.0/24", "direct"), ("0.0.0.0/0", "10.12.1.254") };
var dojoS = new List<(string Cidr, string Via)> { ("10.12.2.0/24", "direct") };
var dojoSFixed = new List<(string Cidr, string Via)> { ("10.12.2.0/24", "direct"), ("10.12.1.0/24", "10.12.2.254") };
Dojo.Eq("server lacks a route back", "no route back", Ping(dojoC, dojoS, "10.12.1.10", "10.12.2.10"));
Dojo.Eq("client has no gateway", "no route there", Ping(new List<(string Cidr, string Via)> { ("10.12.1.0/24", "direct") }, dojoSFixed, "10.12.1.10", "10.12.2.10"));
hints: Two lookups: client towards server, server towards client.

steps.title: Build it: your first router
prompt: Two networks, one router. In the **Network builder**, connect `192.168.1.0/24` and `192.168.2.0/24` with a router, give its interfaces addresses, and set each PC's default gateway. Then ping across and read every hop.
steps.explain: A PC sends anything outside its own subnet to its default gateway. Without a gateway, or with one in the wrong subnet, the ping never leaves the PC.
